claim: SRSF3 ablation results in the loss of pluripotency.
source: SRSF3 ablation resulting in the loss of pluripotency
evidence: The abstract directly states that SRSF3 ablation results in loss of pluripotency, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: SRSF3 overexpression enhances reprogramming.
source: its overexpression enhancing reprogramming
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 1F showing increased AP-positive colonies.

claim: SRSF3 binds to Nanog mRNA to facilitate its nucleo-cytoplasmic export independent of splicing.
source: Strikingly, SRSF3 binds to the core pluripotency transcription factor Nanog mRNA to facilitate its nucleo-cytoplasmic export independent of splicing.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this mechanism, supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing nuclear retention of Nanog mRNA in SRSF3-depleted cells and export of intronless Nanog constructs.

claim: In the absence of SRSF3 binding, Nanog mRNA is sequestered in the nucleus.
source: In the absence of SRSF3 binding, Nanog mRNA is sequestered in the nucleus and protein levels are severely downregulated.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by subcellular fractionation data in Figure 4C and Figure 4F.

claim: NANOG protein levels are severely downregulated in the absence of SRSF3 binding.
source: In the absence of SRSF3 binding, Nanog mRNA is sequestered in the nucleus and protein levels are severely downregulated.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by Western blot data in Figure 2C showing reduced NANOG protein in SRSF3-depleted iPSCs.

claim: SRSF3 controls the alternative splicing of the export factor Nxf1.
source: Moreover, SRSF3 controls the alternative splicing of the export factor Nxf1 and RNA regulators with established roles in pluripotency
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by RNA-seq and iCLIP data in Figure 6D-F showing SRSF3 binding to and regulation of Nxf1 intron 10.

claim: SRSF3 controls the alternative splicing of RNA regulators with established roles in pluripotency.
source: Moreover, SRSF3 controls the alternative splicing of the export factor Nxf1 and RNA regulators with established roles in pluripotency
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by RNA-seq data showing regulation of Mbnl2 and Fip1l1 splicing in Figure 6G-J.

claim: SRSF3 controls the steady-state levels of mRNAs encoding chromatin modifiers.
source: and the steady-state levels of mRNAs encoding chromatin modifiers
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data in Figure 7D showing altered expression of PRC2 components.

claim: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) can be generated from various cell types by the enforced expression of transcription factors OCT4, KLF4, SOX2 and MYC (OKSM).
source: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) can be generated from various cell types by the enforced expression of transcription factors such as OCT4, KLF4, SOX2 and MYC (OKSM) (Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the seminal work by Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006.

claim: The master transcription factors OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG together with many other factors maintain pluripotency both in iPSCs and embryonic stem cells (ESCs).
source: The master transcription factors OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG together with many other factors maintain pluripotency both in iPSCs and embryonic stem cells (ESCs) derived from the inner cell mass of the blastocyst stage embryo (De Los Angeles et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to De Los Angeles et al., 2015.

claim: ESCs are derived from the inner cell mass of the blastocyst stage embryo.
source: embryonic stem cells (ESCs) derived from the inner cell mass of the blastocyst stage embryo (De Los Angeles et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to De Los Angeles et al., 2015.

claim: Polycomb repressive complex 1 and 2 (PRC1/2) control self-renewal and differentiation potential by repressing lineage-specific genes.
source: Chromatin modifiers, such as the polycomb repressive complex 1 and 2 (PRC1/2), control self-renewal and differentiation potential by repressing lineage-specific genes and they reset the epigenetic landscape during reprogramming (De Los Angeles et al., 2015; Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to De Los Angeles et al., 2015 and Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006.

claim: PRC1/2 reset the epigenetic landscape during reprogramming.
source: Chromatin modifiers, such as the polycomb repressive complex 1 and 2 (PRC1/2), control self-renewal and differentiation potential by repressing lineage-specific genes and they reset the epigenetic landscape during reprogramming (De Los Angeles et al., 2015; Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to De Los Angeles et al., 2015 and Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006.

claim: Global changes in alternative splicing patterns take place during reprogramming.
source: Global changes in alternative splicing (AS) and polyadenylation (APA) patterns take place during reprogramming (Cieply et al., 2016; Ji and Tian, 2009; Lackford et al., 2014; Ohta et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Global changes in polyadenylation patterns take place during reprogramming.
source: Global changes in alternative splicing (AS) and polyadenylation (APA) patterns take place during reprogramming (Cieply et al., 2016; Ji and Tian, 2009; Lackford et al., 2014; Ohta et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: ESCs express more than 500 different RBPs.
source: Remarkably, ESCs express more than 500 different RBPs (Kwon et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kwon et al., 2013.

claim: MBNL1/2 splicing factors act as negative regulators of pluripotency and reprogramming.
source: For instance, MBNL1/2 splicing factors act as negative regulators of pluripotency and reprogramming (Han et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Han et al., 2013.

claim: The ectopic expression of the splicing factor ESRP1 enhances reprogramming.
source: the ectopic expression of the splicing factor ESRP1 enhances reprogramming (Cieply et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cieply et al., 2016.

claim: SRSF2 regulates alternative splicing in human pluripotent stem cells.
source: and SRSF2 regulates alternative splicing in human pluripotent stem cells (Lu et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2014.

claim: FIP1 promotes maintenance of pluripotency by activating ESC-specific APA profiles.
source: FIP1 (encoded by Fip1l1) promotes maintenance of pluripotency by activating ESC-specific APA profiles (Lackford et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lackford et al., 2014.

claim: SRSF3 regulates constitutive and alternative splicing.
source: We and others have previously shown that SRSF3 regulates constitutive and alternative splicing as well as other steps of RNA metabolism (Änkö et al., 2012; Auyeung et al., 2013; Cavaloc et al., 1999; Huang and Steitz, 2001; Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016; Zhong et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: SRSF3 regulates other steps of RNA metabolism.
source: We and others have previously shown that SRSF3 regulates constitutive and alternative splicing as well as other steps of RNA metabolism (Änkö et al., 2012; Auyeung et al., 2013; Cavaloc et al., 1999; Huang and Steitz, 2001; Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016; Zhong et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: SRSF3 expression is regulated during cell cycle.
source: At the cellular level, SRSF3 expression is regulated during cell cycle, SRSF3 overexpression in cancer cells enhances cell proliferation and its depletion leads to a cell cycle arrest (Jia et al., 2010; Jumaa et al., 1997; Kurokawa et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: SRSF3 overexpression in cancer cells enhances cell proliferation.
source: At the cellular level, SRSF3 expression is regulated during cell cycle, SRSF3 overexpression in cancer cells enhances cell proliferation and its depletion leads to a cell cycle arrest (Jia et al., 2010; Jumaa et al., 1997; Kurokawa et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: SRSF3 depletion leads to a cell cycle arrest.
source: At the cellular level, SRSF3 expression is regulated during cell cycle, SRSF3 overexpression in cancer cells enhances cell proliferation and its depletion leads to a cell cycle arrest (Jia et al., 2010; Jumaa et al., 1997; Kurokawa et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Srsf3-null mice fail to form blastocysts.
source: SRSF3 plays a pivotal role during development as Srsf3-null mice fail to form blastocysts (Jumaa et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jumaa et al., 1999.

claim: SRSF3 was identified as a potential regulator of reprogramming in an RNAi screen performed in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs).
source: SRSF3 was also identified as a potential regulator of reprogramming in an RNAi screen performed in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) (Ohta et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ohta et al., 2013.

claim: During reprogramming, Srsf3 mRNA expression was upregulated first at day 3, followed by a sharp increase by day 9.
source: During reprogramming, Srsf3 mRNA expression was upregulated first at day 3, followed by a sharp increase by day 9 (Figure 1B, dotted line).
evidence: This statement is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Srsf3 mRNA levels are significantly higher in ESCs and iPSCs compared to MEFs.
source: Analysis of several independent cell lines revealed significantly higher levels of Srsf3 mRNA in ESCs and iPSCs compared to MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The biphasic increase in Srsf3 expression coincided with the two transcriptional waves of reprogramming.
source: The biphasic increase in Srsf3 expression coincided with the two transcriptional waves of reprogramming (Polo et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by comparison to previously published data on transcriptional waves (Polo et al., 2012) and the expression data in Figure 1B.

claim: Srsf3 mRNA expression increases specifically in cells that successfully formed iPSCs compared to cells refractory to reprogramming.
source: RNA-sequencing data showed an increase in Srsf3 mRNA expression specifically in cells that successfully formed iPSCs compared to cells refractory to reprogramming (Polo et al., 2012) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA-seq data from Polo et al., 2012, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The numbers of AP positive colonies were significantly reduced in SRSF3-depleted cells compared to controls.
source: The numbers of AP positive colonies were significantly reduced in SRSF3-depleted cells compared to controls and untreated (−4OHT) cells (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This statement is supported by AP staining and quantification data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: AP-positive colonies generated from SRSF3-deficient MEFs failed to form teratomas.
source: The few AP-positive colonies that were generated from SRSF3-deficient MEFs consistently failed to form teratomas (n = 5, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This statement is supported by teratoma formation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: SRSF3-depleted cells show strongly reduced expression of Nanog and endogenous Pou5f1 from day 13 onwards when Dox was removed.
source: The failure of SRSF3-depleted cells to induce the pluripotency program was further confirmed by a strongly reduced expression of Nanog and endogenous Pou5f1 (encoding OCT4) from day 13 onwards when Dox - and ectopic OKSM expression - was removed (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This statement is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: SRSF3 depletion does not lead to significant increase in cell death in MEFs during reprogramming.
source: We did not detect significant increase in cell death in SRSF3-deficient MEFs during reprogramming (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), similar to previous observations (Ohta et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by AnnexinV/PI flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and comparison to Ohta et al., 2013.

claim: SRSF3 depletion leads to a systematic reduction in the number of reprogramming cells.
source: We detected a systematic reduction in the number of SRSF3-depleted cells when compared to controls, whereas SRSF3 overexpression led to an increase in cell numbers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This statement is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: SRSF3 overexpression leads to an increase in cell numbers during reprogramming.
source: We detected a systematic reduction in the number of SRSF3-depleted cells when compared to controls, whereas SRSF3 overexpression led to an increase in cell numbers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This statement is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: SRSF3 depletion at day 8 of reprogramming significantly reduces the number of transgene-independent AP positive colonies at day 16.
source: SRSF3 was efficiently depleted following 4OHT treatment by day 9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) and the number of transgene-independent AP positive colonies was significantly reduced at day 16, accompanied by a reduced expression of pluripotency markers (Figure 1E).
evidence: This statement is supported by AP staining and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: SRSF3 is required to activate the pluripotency program during reprogramming.
source: These data demonstrate that SRSF3 is required to activate the pluripotency program during reprogramming.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing reduced AP colonies and pluripotency marker expression when SRSF3 is depleted at different time points during reprogramming.

claim: SRSF3 overexpression in MEFs results in a significantly greater number of AP-positive colonies compared to GFP only controls.
source: SRSF3 overexpression in MEFs resulted in a significantly greater number of AP-positive colonies compared to GFP only controls (Figure 1F).
evidence: This statement is supported by AP staining and quantification data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: SRSF3 overexpression enhances reprogramming efficiency as shown by cell surface marker expression.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of cell surface marker expression at reprogramming days 6 and 16 further supported the enhanced reprogramming efficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This statement is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K.

claim: SRSF3 is not only essential for reprogramming but is also able to boost the generation of AP-positive colonies.
source: This analysis demonstrates that SRSF3 is not only essential for reprogramming but is also able to boost the generation of AP-positive colonies.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined data showing reduced reprogramming with SRSF3 depletion and enhanced reprogramming with SRSF3 overexpression.

claim: SRSF3 depletion leads to a rapid loss of iPSC colony morphology.
source: Light microscopic inspection showed a rapid loss of iPSC colony morphology following SRSF3 depletion (Figure 2B).
evidence: This statement is supported by phase contrast microscopy images shown in Figure 2B.

claim: NANOG protein expression was strongly reduced in SRSF3-deficient iPSCs.
source: NANOG protein expression was strongly reduced in SRSF3-deficient iPSCs (Figure 2C)
evidence: This statement is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Nanog mRNA levels were little affected by SRSF3 depletion in iPSCs.
source: Surprisingly, Nanog mRNA levels were little affected while the expression of other pluripotency genes such as Pou5f1 (encoding OCT4), Sox2, Klf4, Zfp42 (encoding REX1) and Myc was strongly reduced (Figure 2D).
evidence: This statement is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The expression of Pou5f1, Sox2, Klf4, Zfp42 and Myc was strongly reduced in SRSF3-deficient iPSCs.
source: Surprisingly, Nanog mRNA levels were little affected while the expression of other pluripotency genes such as Pou5f1 (encoding OCT4), Sox2, Klf4, Zfp42 (encoding REX1) and Myc was strongly reduced (Figure 2D).
evidence: This statement is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SRSF3 depletion in iPSCs leads to a reduction in cell numbers.
source: Similar to MEFs, SRSF3 depletion in iPSCs led to a reduction in cell numbers (Figure 2E).
evidence: This statement is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The level of AnnexinV/PI-negative cells was reduced in SRSF3-depleted iPSCs compared to controls.
source: Whereas SRSF3-deficient MEFs showed no cell death, the level of AnnexinV/PI-negative cells was reduced in SRSF3-depleted iPSCs compared to controls, indicative of an increase in apoptosis (Figure 2F).
evidence: This statement is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: SRSF3 depletion leads to exit from pluripotency even in the absence of apoptosis.
source: Even in the absence of apoptosis, SRSF3 depletion led to a stark increase in the number of differentiating colonies and reduction in the expression of pluripotency markers (Figure 2G–I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B), demonstrating that SRSF3 directly contributed to the maintenance of pluripotency.
evidence: This statement is supported by colony morphology assessment and RT-qPCR data in QVD-treated cells shown in Figure 2G-I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: SRSF3 depletion does not result in increased γH2Ax levels marking DNA double stranded breaks.
source: In support of this and unlike SRSF1 and SRSF2 (Li and Manley, 2005; Xiao et al., 2007), SRSF3 depletion did not result in increased γH2Ax levels marking DNA double stranded breaks (Figure 2H), suggesting that SRSF3 loss does not lead to genomic instability.
evidence: This statement is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2H and comparison to previous studies on SRSF1 and SRSF2.

claim: SRSF3 loss does not lead to genomic instability.
source: In support of this and unlike SRSF1 and SRSF2 (Li and Manley, 2005; Xiao et al., 2007), SRSF3 depletion did not result in increased γH2Ax levels marking DNA double stranded breaks (Figure 2H), suggesting that SRSF3 loss does not lead to genomic instability.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the absence of γH2Ax increase shown in Figure 2H.

claim: SRSF3 is essential for self-renewing cells.
source: These data demonstrate an essential role for SRSF3 in self-renewing cells, loss of SRSF3 leading to exit from pluripotency independent of cell death.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined data showing loss of pluripotency markers and colony morphology even when apoptosis is inhibited.

claim: The cellular phenotype of SRSF3-depleted pluripotent cells resembles that of Nanog-null cells.
source: Consistent with this, the cellular phenotype of SRSF3-depleted pluripotent cells resembled that of Nanog-null cells (Mitsui et al., 2003).
evidence: This comparison is based on the observed phenotypes and supported by citation to Mitsui et al., 2003.

claim: The pooled SRSF3-GFP iCLIP reads yielded 3.3M unique crosslink sites.
source: The pooled SRSF3-GFP iCLIP reads yielded 3.3M unique crosslink sites compared to 51K in the control while the anti-SRSR3 iCLIP resulted in low read coverage, suggesting a poor affinity of the antibody to RNA-bound SRSF3 (Figure 3—source data 3, Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by iCLIP sequencing data reported in Figure 3—source data 3 and 4.

claim: The control iCLIP yielded 51K unique crosslink sites.
source: The pooled SRSF3-GFP iCLIP reads yielded 3.3M unique crosslink sites compared to 51K in the control while the anti-SRSR3 iCLIP resulted in low read coverage, suggesting a poor affinity of the antibody to RNA-bound SRSF3 (Figure 3—source data 3, Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by iCLIP sequencing data reported in Figure 3—source data 3 and 4.

claim: The anti-SRSF3 antibody has poor affinity to RNA-bound SRSF3.
source: The pooled SRSF3-GFP iCLIP reads yielded 3.3M unique crosslink sites compared to 51K in the control while the anti-SRSR3 iCLIP resulted in low read coverage, suggesting a poor affinity of the antibody to RNA-bound SRSF3 (Figure 3—source data 3, Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the low read coverage obtained with the anti-SRSF3 antibody compared to SRSF3-GFP.

claim: 219K significant SRSF3-GFP crosslink sites were identified in the pluripotent transcriptome.
source: Significant crosslink sites were identified as previously described (FDR < 0.05, (Änkö et al., 2012; König et al., 2010)), resulting in 219K SRSF3-GFP sites in the pluripotent transcriptome (Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by iCLIP data analysis reported in Figure 3—source data 4.

claim: The SRSF3 consensus binding motif is consistent with previous SRSF3-GFP iCLIP and in vitro studies.
source: The consensus binding motif was consistent with previous SRSF3-GFP iCLIP and in vitro studies (Figure 3B) (Änkö et al., 2012; Hargous et al., 2006; Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the motif shown in Figure 3B and comparison to previous studies.

claim: There is a high overlap (74%) between anti-SRSF3 and SRSF3-GFP CLIP sites.
source: The consensus binding motifs of anti-SRSF3 and SRSF3-GFP iCLIPs were identical (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and there was a high overlap (74%) between anti-SRSF3 and SRSF3-GFP CLIP sites, consistent with previous studies demonstrating the functionality of SRSF3-GFP (Ankö et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by comparison of iCLIP data and citation to Ankö et al., 2010.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis of genes with significant SRSF3 binding sites showed an enrichment in functions related to RNA metabolism.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of genes with significant SRSF3 binding sites showed an enrichment in functions related to RNA metabolism (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), supporting previous observations (Änkö et al., 2012; Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and comparison to previous studies.

claim: SRSF3 binding sites are enriched in genes associated with chromatin modifications, transcriptional regulation, cell division/cycle and DNA damage response.
source: Importantly, we detected an enrichment across GO terms associated with chromatin modifications, transcriptional regulation, cell division/cycle and DNA damage response (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), which are central functions in the establishment and maintenance of pluripotent cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: SRSF3 binds to RNAs encoding key pluripotency regulators including Nanog, Pou5f1, Zfp42, Klf4, Sox2 and Myc.
source: SRSF3 bound to a large number of (pre-)mRNAs encoding pluripotency transcription factors (Figure 3D), including Nanog, Pou5f1, Zfp42, Klf4, Sox2 and Myc that were downregulated in SRSF3 depleted iPSCs (see Figure 2D).
evidence: This statement is supported by iCLIP data shown in Figure 3D and correlation with expression data in Figure 2D.

claim: SRSF3 binds to RNAs encoding chromatin modifiers including components of PRC2.
source: Significant SRSF3-binding sites were also detected in RNAs encoding chromatin modifiers (Figure 3D) such as the components of PRC2 required to deposit repressive histone-3 lysine-27 tri-methyl (H3K27me3) marks in self-renewing cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by iCLIP data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SRSF3 binds to RNAs encoding RBPs with previously assigned roles in reprogramming and/or pluripotent cells.
source: Interestingly, SRSF3 bound to RNAs encoding RBPs with previously assigned roles in reprogramming and/or pluripotent cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This statement is supported by iCLIP data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The pluripotency related SRSF3 RNA targets form an interconnected network.
source: Functional protein association network analysis by STRING (Szklarczyk et al., 2015) showed that the pluripotency related - as defined by (Chen and Hu, 2017; Young, 2011) - SRSF3 RNA targets formed an interconnected network while SRSF3 has not been previously assigned as part of this network (Figure 3E)
evidence: This statement is supported by STRING network analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: SRSF3 has not been previously assigned as part of the pluripotency network.
source: Functional protein association network analysis by STRING (Szklarczyk et al., 2015) showed that the pluripotency related - as defined by (Chen and Hu, 2017; Young, 2011) - SRSF3 RNA targets formed an interconnected network while SRSF3 has not been previously assigned as part of this network (Figure 3E)
evidence: This statement is supported by STRING network analysis shown in Figure 3E and comparison to previous literature.

claim: Nanog gene produces three annotated splice variants.
source: Although Nanog gene produces three annotated splice variants, only one of the variants was significantly expressed in iPSCs based on our RNA-seq data (Figure 4A).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only one Nanog splice variant is significantly expressed in iPSCs.
source: Although Nanog gene produces three annotated splice variants, only one of the variants was significantly expressed in iPSCs based on our RNA-seq data (Figure 4A).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The predominantly expressed Nanog variant encodes the full-length NANOG protein.
source: This variant encodes the full-length (FL) NANOG protein, whereas the two other splice variants produce an N-terminally truncated (TR) isoform.
evidence: This statement is based on the gene structure shown in Figure 4A and knowledge of the coding potential of the variants.

claim: SRSF3 depletion does not affect the first exon choice of Nanog mRNA.
source: RT-qPCR analysis showed that SRSF3 depletion did not affect the first exon choice of Nanog mRNA (Figure 4B).
evidence: This statement is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Nanog was predicted as one of ~400 mRNAs whose nucleo-cytoplasmic export was affected by SRSF3 knockdown in P19 cells.
source: A previous study in P19 cells predicted Nanog as one of ~400 mRNAs whose nucleo-cytoplasmic export was affected by SRSF3 knockdown (Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016.

claim: The direct interaction of SRSF3 with the nuclear export factor NXF1 is well-documented.
source: The direct interaction of SRSF3 with the nuclear export factor NXF1 is well-documented (Huang et al., 2003; Huang and Steitz, 2001; Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Subcellular fractionation revealed nuclear accumulation of Nanog mRNA in SRSF3 depleted iPSCs.
source: Accordingly, subcellular fractionation revealed nuclear accumulation of Nanog mRNA in SRSF3 depleted iPSCs (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This statement is supported by subcellular fractionation and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: SRSF3 binding to WT-Nanog is strongly reduced when SRSF3-binding sites are mutated.
source: As expected, RNA immunoprecipitation showed strongly reduced binding of SRSF3 to ΔSRSF3-Nanog mRNA (Figure 4E).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ΔSRSF3-Nanog mRNA lacking SRSF3-binding sites is retained in the nucleus in both control and SRSF3-deficient cells.
source: Nucleo-cytoplasmic fractionation demonstrated that ΔSRSF3-Nanog mRNA lacking SRSF3-binding sites was retained in the nucleus both in control and SRSF3-deficient cells (Figure 4F, dotted bars).
evidence: This statement is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The intronless mRNA produced from the WT-Nanog construct is efficiently exported in control cells.
source: The intronless mRNA produced from the WT-Nanog construct was efficiently exported in control cells while it was retained in the nucleus in SRSF3-depleted iPSCs (Figure 4F, compare white and black bars).
evidence: This statement is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The intronless WT-Nanog mRNA is retained in the nucleus in SRSF3-depleted iPSCs.
source: The intronless mRNA produced from the WT-Nanog construct was efficiently exported in control cells while it was retained in the nucleus in SRSF3-depleted iPSCs (Figure 4F, compare white and black bars).
evidence: This statement is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: SRSF3 binding is essential for Nanog mRNA export.
source: This demonstrates firstly, that SRSF3 binding is essential for Nanog mRNA export and secondly, that SRSF3 activity in Nanog mRNA export is independent of pre-mRNA splicing.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing that intronless WT-Nanog is exported in control cells but retained when SRSF3 is depleted or when SRSF3-binding sites are mutated.

claim: SRSF3 activity in Nanog mRNA export is independent of pre-mRNA splicing.
source: This demonstrates firstly, that SRSF3 binding is essential for Nanog mRNA export and secondly, that SRSF3 activity in Nanog mRNA export is independent of pre-mRNA splicing.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing that intronless WT-Nanog mRNA requires SRSF3 for export.

claim: NXF1 binds to WT-Nanog mRNA in HEK293 cells.
source: RNA immunoprecipitation with an anti-NXF1 antibody showed NXF1 binding to WT-Nanog mRNA while in the absence SRSF3-binding sites the Nanog-NXF1 interaction was abolished (Figure 4G, left αNXF1 IP; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The Nanog-NXF1 interaction is abolished in the absence of SRSF3-binding sites.
source: RNA immunoprecipitation with an anti-NXF1 antibody showed NXF1 binding to WT-Nanog mRNA while in the absence SRSF3-binding sites the Nanog-NXF1 interaction was abolished (Figure 4G, left αNXF1 IP; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: SRSF3 binding is required for the association of NXF1 with Nanog mRNA.
source: RNA immunoprecipitation with an anti-NXF1 antibody showed NXF1 binding to WT-Nanog mRNA while in the absence SRSF3-binding sites the Nanog-NXF1 interaction was abolished (Figure 4G, left αNXF1 IP; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), demonstrating that SRSF3 binding is required for the association of NXF1 with Nanog mRNA.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the RNA immunoprecipitation data showing loss of NXF1 binding when SRSF3 sites are mutated.

claim: SRSF3 depletion led to a change in 281 annotated AS events.
source: Using a cut-off of ΔPSI≥|0.2| and Bayes factor ≥5, SRSF3 depletion led to a change in 281 annotated AS events, of which the skipped exon (SE) was the most affected category, both in terms of absolute numbers and proportion of assessed events (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by MISO analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Skipped exon (SE) was the most affected AS category following SRSF3 depletion.
source: Using a cut-off of ΔPSI≥|0.2| and Bayes factor ≥5, SRSF3 depletion led to a change in 281 annotated AS events, of which the skipped exon (SE) was the most affected category, both in terms of absolute numbers and proportion of assessed events (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by MISO analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: More exons showed increase in skipping following SRSF3 depletion.
source: Overall, more exons showed increase in skipping following SRSF3 depletion, in agreement with the role of many SR proteins in enhancing exon inclusion.
evidence: This statement is based on the AS analysis and comparison to known SR protein functions.

claim: Sixty-one percent of the altered AS events had associated SRSF3-binding sites within the transcript region.
source: Sixty-one percent of the altered AS events had associated SRSF3-binding sites within the transcript region based on our iCLIP data.
evidence: This statement is based on integration of iCLIP and RNA-seq data.

claim: SRSF3 binding is enriched within regulated exons.
source: SRSF3 binding was enriched within the regulated exons, with few sites also mapping up- and downstream (Figure 5B).
evidence: This statement is supported by mapping of iCLIP sites to regulated exons shown in Figure 5B.

claim: SRSF3 binding within the regulated exon or intron enhances inclusion across the AS types.
source: Inspection of SRSF3-binding sites around exons decreasing in inclusion in SRSF3 depleted cells suggested that SRSF3 binding within the regulated exon or intron enhances inclusion across the AS types (SE, IR, A5SS and A3SS) which is in accordance with SRSF3-binding sites acting as splicing enhancers (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is supported by analysis of SRSF3-binding site positions relative to regulated AS events shown in Figure 5C.

claim: AS changes during reprogramming show a gradual increase from MEFs to iPSCs.
source: We first determined cumulative changes in AS during reprogramming using MISO by comparing each of the time points to MEFs, which showed a gradual increase in AS from MEFs to iPSCs (Figure 5D, top panel) similar to previous reports (Cieply et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by MISO analysis shown in Figure 5D and comparison to previous studies.

claim: AS changes during reprogramming take place in two waves.
source: Sequential comparisons between the time points revealed, however, that AS changes during reprogramming took place in two waves similar to transcriptional changes (Polo et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by sequential MISO analysis and comparison to transcriptional wave data from Polo et al., 2012.

claim: Major AS pattern alterations occur early between MEFs and day 3, and late between day 12 and iPSC.
source: The apparent increase in AS towards iPSCs reflected major AS pattern alterations early between MEFs and day 3, and late between day 12 and iPSC (Figure 5D, bottom panel).
evidence: This statement is supported by sequential MISO analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Skipped exons were the major AS type across the reprogramming time course.
source: When analysing the different types of AS events in the course of reprogramming, skipped exons were the major type across the time course although all AS types, including intron retention, were dynamically regulated during reprogramming (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Figure 5—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by MISO analysis shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All AS types, including intron retention, are dynamically regulated during reprogramming.
source: When analysing the different types of AS events in the course of reprogramming, skipped exons were the major type across the time course although all AS types, including intron retention, were dynamically regulated during reprogramming (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Figure 5—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by MISO analysis shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Principal component analysis shows molecular connectivity reflecting the progression from MEFs to iPSCs.
source: Principal component analysis showed a molecular connectivity reflecting the progression from MEFs to iPSCs (Figure 6A), reminiscent but independent of the connectivity at the transcriptome level (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B) (Polo et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The number of regulated RNA features increases from MEFs to iPSC when compared to MEFs.
source: Similar to the analysis of annotated AS events using MISO, the number of regulated RNA features identified by JunctionSeq increased from MEFs to iPSC when each of the reprogramming intermediates was compared to MEFs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by JunctionSeq analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The majority of RNA processing changes occur at only two time points during reprogramming.
source: Sequential comparisons between each consecutive time point further demonstrated that the majority of RNA processing changes occurred at only two time points (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), coinciding with the biphasic increase in Srsf3 expression (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by sequential JunctionSeq analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and correlation with Srsf3 expression data.

claim: 53% of SARFs are grouped within 3 out of 20 clusters showing similar upwards trajectory towards iPSCs.
source: Unsupervised k-means clustering grouped 53% of SARFs within 3 out of 20 clusters, each showing a similar upwards trajectory towards iPSCs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This statement is supported by k-means clustering analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: SRSF3 binding is associated with splicing changes contributing to the commitment to the pluripotent cell fate during reprogramming.
source: This examination shows that SRSF3 binding is associated with splicing changes contributing to the commitment to the pluripotent cell fate during reprogramming.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the clustering analysis showing enrichment of SRSF3-associated features in clusters with trajectories towards iPSCs.

claim: SRSF3-binding sites are detected in 37% of regulated DIs in contrast to only 27% of non-regulated DIs.
source: SRSF3-binding sites were found in 37% of regulated DIs in contrast to only 27% of non-regulated DIs (Figure 6C,iii).
evidence: This statement is supported by analysis of SRSF3-binding sites in DIs shown in Figure 6C.

claim: SRSF3-binding sites are detected within DI regions of Nxf1 pre-mRNA.
source: Indeed, SRSF3-binding sites were detected within DI regions of RNA regulators such as Nxf1 pre-mRNA (Figure 6D).
evidence: This statement is supported by iCLIP data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Nxf1 intron 10 is dynamically regulated during reprogramming.
source: SRSF3-binding sites mapped to Nxf1 intron 10, which was classified as DI and dynamically regulated during reprogramming (Figure 6D–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6D-E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Up to 40% intron retention is detected in Nxf1 in reprogramming intermediates.
source: Although the level of intron containing Nxf1 mRNA was similar in MEFs and iPSCs, up to 40% intron retention was detected in the reprogramming intermediates (Figure 6E).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: SRSF3 ablation leads to a decrease in the level of intron 10 containing Nxf1 mRNA.
source: SRSF3 ablation led to a decrease in the level of intron 10 containing Nxf1 mRNA (Figure 6F), suggesting that SRSF3 binding is required for the dynamic changes in Nxf1-Int10 retention during reprogramming.
evidence: This statement is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: SRSF3 binding is required for the dynamic changes in Nxf1-Int10 retention during reprogramming.
source: SRSF3 ablation led to a decrease in the level of intron 10 containing Nxf1 mRNA (Figure 6F), suggesting that SRSF3 binding is required for the dynamic changes in Nxf1-Int10 retention during reprogramming.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the data showing reduced intron retention when SRSF3 is depleted.

claim: The intron 10 containing Nxf1 transcript encodes a short isoform of NXF1 protein that can bind to RNA but cannot interact with the nuclear pore complex.
source: The intron 10 containing Nxf1 transcript encodes a short isoform of NXF1 protein that can bind to RNA but cannot interact with the nuclear pore complex (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Li et al., 2016.

claim: NXF1 binds to Nxf1 intron 10 to allow for the efficient export of the intron containing mRNA.
source: NXF1 has been shown to bind to this intron to allow for the efficient export of the intron containing mRNA (Li et al., 2006; Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Li et al., 2006 and Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016.

claim: SRSF3 may affect mRNA export more broadly by regulating NXF1 isoform expression and function through Nxf1 intron 10.
source: Therefore, SRSF3 does not only act as an export adaptor of distinct mRNAs as exemplified by Nanog mRNA in pluripotent cells but also it may affect mRNA export more broadly by regulating NXF1 isoform expression and function through Nxf1 intron 10.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the data showing SRSF3 regulation of Nxf1 intron 10 retention and the known function of the resulting NXF1 isoform.

claim: A quarter of SARFs that are DIs flank alternative exons that are regulated during reprogramming.
source: Further assessment of these and other SARFs that were DIs showed a quarter of them flanking alternative exons that were regulated during reprogramming (Figure 6D, iv).
evidence: This statement is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The inclusion of AS exons flanking DIs is dynamically regulated during reprogramming.
source: The inclusion of the AS exons flanking DIs was dynamically regulated during reprogramming (Figure 6I and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6I and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: SRSF3 ablation leads to changes in the inclusion of AS exons flanking DIs.
source: and SRSF3 ablation led to changes in their inclusion (Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The alternative exon in Srsf3 itself is flanked by DIs.
source: Of note, the alternative exon in Srsf3 itself is flanked by DIs and we and others have previously shown that SRSF3 autoregulates the splicing of this exon (Änkö et al., 2012; Lareau et al., 2007; Ni et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies showing SRSF3 autoregulation.

claim: SRSF3 autoregulates the splicing of its alternative exon.
source: Of note, the alternative exon in Srsf3 itself is flanked by DIs and we and others have previously shown that SRSF3 autoregulates the splicing of this exon (Änkö et al., 2012; Lareau et al., 2007; Ni et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The splicing of DIs provides a regulatory step in gene expression during reprogramming.
source: These data show that the splicing of DIs provide a regulatory step in gene expression during reprogramming and demonstrates a role for SRSF3 in splicing of rate limiting DIs in pluripotent cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing dynamic regulation of DIs during reprogramming and SRSF3's role in regulating them.

claim: SRSF3 plays a role in splicing of rate limiting DIs in pluripotent cells.
source: These data show that the splicing of DIs provide a regulatory step in gene expression during reprogramming and demonstrates a role for SRSF3 in splicing of rate limiting DIs in pluripotent cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing SRSF3 binding to and regulation of DIs.

claim: 803 differentially expressed genes were identified following SRSF3 depletion in pluripotent cells.
source: In pluripotent cells, we identified 803 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) following SRSF3 depletion (482 up- and 321 downregulated, FDR < 0.05, log|FC| ≥ 1) (Figure 7A and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 482 genes were upregulated following SRSF3 depletion in pluripotent cells.
source: In pluripotent cells, we identified 803 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) following SRSF3 depletion (482 up- and 321 downregulated, FDR < 0.05, log|FC| ≥ 1) (Figure 7A and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 321 genes were downregulated following SRSF3 depletion in pluripotent cells.
source: In pluripotent cells, we identified 803 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) following SRSF3 depletion (482 up- and 321 downregulated, FDR < 0.05, log|FC| ≥ 1) (Figure 7A and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 44% of DEGs have SRSF3 binding sites within transcript region.
source: Forty-four percent of DEGs had SRSF3 binding sites within transcript region (351 of 802), with no difference between genes that were up- (43%) or downregulated (45%).
evidence: This statement is supported by integration of iCLIP and RNA-seq data.

claim: SRSF3 regulates gene expression including its own mRNA abundance via NMD surveillance pathway.
source: SRSF3 has been reported to regulate gene expression including its own mRNA abundance via NMD surveillance pathway (Änkö et al., 2012; Lareau et al., 2007; Ni et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Almost half of the NMD-regulated genes/mRNAs have SRSF3-binding sites.
source: We compared the SRSF3 CLIP RNA targets to previously identified transcripts regulated by NMD in mouse ESCs (Hurt et al., 2013). This revealed that almost half of the NMD-regulated genes/mRNAs had SRSF3-binding sites, suggesting that SRSF3-mediated RNA regulation may be broadly linked to NMD (Figure 7B).
evidence: This statement is supported by comparison of iCLIP data to NMD-regulated transcripts from Hurt et al., 2013, shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SRSF3-mediated RNA regulation may be broadly linked to NMD.
source: We compared the SRSF3 CLIP RNA targets to previously identified transcripts regulated by NMD in mouse ESCs (Hurt et al., 2013). This revealed that almost half of the NMD-regulated genes/mRNAs had SRSF3-binding sites, suggesting that SRSF3-mediated RNA regulation may be broadly linked to NMD (Figure 7B).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the high overlap between SRSF3 targets and NMD-regulated transcripts.

claim: DEGs with SRSF3-binding sites are enriched in the set of genes/mRNAs regulated by NMD.
source: Further analysis demonstrated that DEGs with SRSF3-binding sites were enriched in the set of genes/mRNAs regulated by NMD (Figure 7C).
evidence: This statement is supported by analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The expression of multiple components of PRC2 is altered in SRSF3-deficient cells.
source: The expression of multiple components of PRC2 was altered in SRSF3-deficient cells (Figure 7D)
evidence: This statement is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: H3K27me3 levels are globally reduced in SRSF3-deficient cells.
source: and consistent with this, the H3K27me3 levels were globally reduced (Figure 7E).
evidence: This statement is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Ezh2 is among the NMD-sensitive SRSF3-bound mRNAs.
source: Ezh2 encoding the histone-lysine methyltransferase of PRC2 was among the NMD-sensitive SRSF3-bound mRNAs.
evidence: This statement is based on integration of iCLIP data and NMD-regulated transcript data.

claim: Only the full-length Ezh2 variant is prominently expressed in pluripotent cells.
source: Based on Ensembl gene annotation and previous studies (Shirahata-Adachi et al., 2017), Ezh2 produces at least three transcript variants, one of which terminates at exon 7. Only the full-length (Ex1-20) variant was prominently expressed in pluripotent cells and SRSF3 binding sites were deposited along this mRNA (Figure 7F).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA-seq and iCLIP data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The level of full-length Ezh2 mRNA is increased by NMD inhibition.
source: The total level of Ezh2 determined by primers spanning exons 2–3 (Ex2-3) was not affected by NMD inhibition, whereas the level of the full-length Ezh2 measured by primers spanning Ex19-20 was increased (Figure 7F).
evidence: This statement is supported by RT-qPCR data after CHX treatment shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The full-length Ezh2 mRNA is downregulated in Srsf3-KO iPSCs.
source: Intriguingly, the full-length Ezh2 mRNA was downregulated in Srsf3-KO iPSCs (Figure 7F), providing evidence that SRSF3 specifically regulates the NMD-sensitive Ezh2 variant.
evidence: This statement is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: SRSF3 specifically regulates the NMD-sensitive Ezh2 variant.
source: Intriguingly, the full-length Ezh2 mRNA was downregulated in Srsf3-KO iPSCs (Figure 7F), providing evidence that SRSF3 specifically regulates the NMD-sensitive Ezh2 variant.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing selective downregulation of the full-length variant in SRSF3-depleted cells.

claim: NMD inhibition increases the level of intronless Epop mRNA.
source: NMD inhibition increased and SRSF3 depletion decreased also the level of the intronless Epop mRNA encoding an ESC specific component of PRC2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This statement is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SRSF3 depletion decreases the level of intronless Epop mRNA.
source: NMD inhibition increased and SRSF3 depletion decreased also the level of the intronless Epop mRNA encoding an ESC specific component of PRC2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This statement is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SRSF3 controls the expression of multiple components of the PRC2 complex.
source: NMD inhibition increased and SRSF3 depletion decreased also the level of the intronless Epop mRNA encoding an ESC specific component of PRC2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that SRSF3 controls the expression of multiple components of the PRC2 complex.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing SRSF3 regulation of Ezh2 and Epop expression.

claim: SRSF3 binds to and regulates the expression of a distinct NMD-sensitive variant of Dnmt3a.
source: Similar to Ezh2, SRSF3 bound to and regulated the expression of a distinct NMD-sensitive variant of Dnmt3a (Dnmt3a-AltEx1) (Figure 7G).
evidence: This statement is supported by iCLIP and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: None of the investigated NMD-sensitive transcript variants contain premature termination codons.
source: Interestingly, none of the investigated transcript variants contained premature termination codons (PTCs) generally associated with mRNAs targeted to NMD.
evidence: This statement is based on examination of the transcript structures shown in the figures.

claim: The half-lives of NMD-sensitive mRNAs are not significantly altered following SRSF3 depletion.
source: The half-lives of the NMD-sensitive mRNAs were not significantly altered following SRSF3 depletion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that SRSF3 regulates the generation of distinct mRNAs whose steady-state levels are maintained by NMD to balance production and turnover.
evidence: This statement is supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: SRSF3 regulates the generation of distinct mRNAs whose steady-state levels are maintained by NMD to balance production and turnover.
source: The half-lives of the NMD-sensitive mRNAs were not significantly altered following SRSF3 depletion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that SRSF3 regulates the generation of distinct mRNAs whose steady-state levels are maintained by NMD to balance production and turnover.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the data showing unchanged mRNA half-lives but altered steady-state levels.

claim: SRSF3 regulates the abundance of chromatin modifiers through binding to distinct NMD-sensitive transcript variants.
source: Taken together, SRSF3 regulates the abundance of chromatin modifiers through binding to distinct NMD-sensitive transcript variants, SRSF3 depletion leading to global changes in the chromatin state of pluripotent stem cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined data showing SRSF3 regulation of PRC2 components and Dnmt3a, and the resulting changes in H3K27me3 levels.

claim: SRSF3 depletion leads to global changes in the chromatin state of pluripotent stem cells.
source: Taken together, SRSF3 regulates the abundance of chromatin modifiers through binding to distinct NMD-sensitive transcript variants, SRSF3 depletion leading to global changes in the chromatin state of pluripotent stem cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing reduced H3K27me3 levels following SRSF3 depletion.
